case.request: Our dispatch team wants customers to get an SMS when their driver is two stops away. We already send delivery-confirmation texts through the existing Twilio integration, so reuse that sender and the template system. Message text: 'Your driver is about 2 stops away. Track your delivery: {tracking_link}'. Rules: send at most once per delivery, only between 7am and 9pm in the recipient's local time, and only to customers with the existing sms_opt_in flag set. If the route is resequenced after the text went out, do not send a second one. Please add a daily count of these messages to the existing notifications report. Done means opted-out customers never receive it and the report shows zero duplicate sends.
case.rationale: Trigger, content, channel, consent rule, time window and dedup behaviour are all stated, so only implementation detail remains.

requirements: Send the customer an SMS when their driver is two stops away from the customer's delivery.
Send the SMS by reusing the existing Twilio integration sender and the existing template system that deliver the delivery-confirmation texts.
The message text must be 'Your driver is about 2 stops away. Track your delivery: {tracking_link}', with {tracking_link} replaced by the delivery's tracking link.
Send the two-stops-away SMS at most once per delivery.
Send the SMS only between 7am and 9pm in the recipient's local time.
Send the SMS only to customers whose existing sms_opt_in flag is set.
If the route is resequenced after the SMS has been sent for a delivery, do not send a second SMS for that delivery.
Add a daily count of two-stops-away SMS messages to the existing notifications report.
Acceptance: opted-out customers never receive the two-stops-away SMS.
Acceptance: the notifications report shows zero duplicate sends of the two-stops-away SMS.
Evaluate the customer's sms_opt_in flag at send time, immediately before handing the message to the Twilio sender, so a customer who opts out after the trigger is not messaged.

Persist a per-delivery record of the two-stops-away SMS send, enforced atomically so concurrent or repeated triggers (including after resequencing) cannot produce a second send, and usable as the data source for the daily count and duplicate check.

The new send path must not be able to send messages in production until the opt-in check, the local-time window check and the once-per-delivery enforcement are all active (for example, keep it disabled behind a flag until they ship together).

blocking_questions.question: What exactly counts as 'two stops away', and which system or event signals it (e.g., dispatch/route stop completion events, remaining-stop count in the route sequence, a telematics feed)? Do skipped, failed or cancelled stops count?
blocking_questions.why: This defines the core trigger for the feature. Without it, the implementer cannot build or objectively verify when the SMS fires.

blocking_questions.question: When the two-stops-away condition occurs outside 7am-9pm recipient local time, should the SMS be suppressed entirely for that delivery or deferred until the window opens (and, if deferred, sent only if the delivery is still pending)?
blocking_questions.why: This is a customer-facing compliance behavior that changes what is built. Neither option is stated in the source, so it should not be chosen by default.

blocking_questions.question: What is the authoritative source of the recipient's local time zone (customer profile, delivery address, phone number area code, depot time zone), and what should happen when it is unknown?
blocking_questions.why: Compliance with the send window depends directly on correctly determining the recipient's local time.

review_findings: Q4 (what counts as 'two stops away' and which event source signals it) is marked non-blocking, but it defines the core trigger for R1. W1 says to 'implement against the answer recorded for Q4', yet no answer exists. W1-AC1 and W1-AC2 cannot be verified objectively until Q4 is resolved. Q4 should be blocking, or W1 should be gated on its resolution.

Q2 (suppress or defer triggers that fall outside 7am-9pm) is marked non-blocking. It is a customer-facing compliance behavior decision. W3 tells the implementer to 'implement per the recorded answers and do not choose silently', but no answer exists, so W3 is not implementable as written. The why_it_matters text also suggests suppression as a default, which amounts to an unrecorded assumption. Q3 (time zone source) likewise directly determines whether R5 is compliant. Both should be blocking, or an explicit approved default should be recorded.

The source says 'between 7am and 9pm' without defining the boundaries. W3-AC2 asserts that 9:00pm is exclusive and 7:00am is inclusive. It labels this directly_stated, but it is an unrecorded inference. The boundary semantics should be captured as an open question or a human decision.

W3-AC3 requires reconciling sent records against opt-in state at send time. No requirement or work item captures a historical or send-time snapshot of sms_opt_in. The criterion also depends on a week of production data after release, so it cannot gate completion of the ticket. The needed data capture should be added as a requirement, and pre-merge verification should be separated from post-release monitoring.

W2 delivers a working send path through the existing Twilio sender and depends only on W1. The opt-in and quiet-hours gate (W3) and deduplication (W4) come afterward. If W2 is merged or deployed alone, opted-out customers could be messaged, sends could fall outside allowed hours, or duplicates could occur. The dependency order should make the send path unreachable until W3 and W4 land, for example through a feature flag or reversed dependencies.

S9 requires that 'the report shows zero duplicate sends'. R8 and W5 add only a daily count, and W5 says duplicates 'can be checked'. It is unclear whether the report itself must display a duplicate metric. W5-AC2 relies on an external reconciliation query plus a screenshot rather than a report field.

The failure semantics of W4's check-and-insert are unspecified. If the sent record is inserted before a Twilio send that then fails, the customer never gets the message. If it is inserted after the send, a crash or race can produce duplicates. The requirements also do not say whether failed sends count as a send for the once-per-delivery rule. Q6 covers this only for reporting, not for the dedup rule.

W1-AC1 requires 'exactly one trigger event' per delivery, while W4 assumes the trigger can fire multiple times (for example after resequencing) and deduplicates at send. The responsibility for once-only behavior is split and contradictory. W1 should allow repeat triggers and leave uniqueness to W4, or the scope should be clarified.

Several criterion provenance labels do not match their sources. W3-AC1 is labeled directly_stated but relies on R11, which is safe_inference; the source only says opted-out customers never receive it. W2-AC2 is classified as automated_test but requires a manual code review note.

case.request: Teachers keep asking for a way to get grades out of the LMS for their own records. Add an 'Export CSV' button to the class gradebook page. The file should have one row per enrolled student with columns: student name, student ID, then one column per assignment (assignment title as header, numeric score or blank if not submitted), and a final column with the current overall percentage. Only the class's assigned teachers and school admins can see the button; students and parents cannot. File name should be the class code plus today's date. It should respect the existing rule that dropped students are hidden from the gradebook.
case.rationale: Format, columns, access and filtering rules are explicit; the only open points are cosmetic.

requirements: The class gradebook page displays an 'Export CSV' button that downloads the class's grades as a CSV file.
The exported CSV contains exactly one row per enrolled student in the class.
CSV columns are, in order: student name, student ID, one column per assignment, and a final column with the student's current overall percentage.
Each assignment column uses the assignment title as its header and contains the student's numeric score, or is blank if the student has not submitted the assignment.
The 'Export CSV' button is visible only to the class's assigned teachers and school admins; students and parents cannot see it.

The export endpoint/action enforces the same authorization server-side, rejecting export requests from anyone other than the class's assigned teachers and school admins (hiding the button alone is not sufficient).
The downloaded file name is the class code plus today's date.
Students who have dropped the class are excluded from the export, consistent with the existing rule that hides dropped students from the gradebook.

work_items.title: Build gradebook CSV content generator (rows, columns, scores, dropped-student exclusion)
work_items.description: Scope: a server-side component that, given a class, produces CSV content for the class's grades. Expected behavior: exactly one row per enrolled student (R2), excluding students who have dropped the class by reusing the existing gradebook rule that hides dropped students rather than re-implementing it (R8). Columns in order: student name, student ID, one column per assignment, then the student's current overall percentage (R3). Each assignment column header is the assignment title; each cell holds the student's numeric score, or is blank if the student has not submitted (R4). Bounded approach: read from the same data source and filtering the gradebook page uses so exported rows and percentages match what the gradebook shows. No repository evidence was supplied, so no file paths, modules or test commands are assumed. Open non-blocking questions to surface to the product owner rather than decide silently: Q2 (ungraded/excused/non-numeric states), Q3 (row/column ordering and duplicate assignment titles), Q5 (percentage formatting and CSV/formula-injection escaping). The chosen handling for these must be documented in the ticket before merge.
criteria: For a class fixture with N enrolled, non-dropped students, the generated CSV contains exactly N data rows plus one header row, and each student appears exactly once.

Header row columns are, in order: student name, student ID, one column per assignment in the class, and a final overall percentage column; each data row's final column equals the student's current overall percentage as shown in the gradebook.
Each assignment column header equals the assignment title; a cell contains the student's numeric score when a score exists and is empty when the student has not submitted.
Students who have dropped the class do not appear in the export, and the exclusion is determined by the same existing rule the gradebook page uses to hide dropped students.

The handling chosen for open questions Q2, Q3 and Q5 (non-numeric/ungraded/excused states, ordering and duplicate titles, percentage formatting and cell escaping) is recorded in the ticket with the product owner's decision or explicitly flagged as pending.

work_items.title: Add authorized gradebook export endpoint with class-code-and-date file name
work_items.description: Scope: a server-side export action/endpoint that invokes the W1 generator and returns the CSV as a file download. Expected behavior: the request is rejected server-side unless the requester is one of the class's assigned teachers or a school admin; students, parents and other users are refused even if they call the endpoint directly (R6). The download file name is the class code plus today's date (R7). Bounded approach: reuse the application's existing authorization/role checks for class teachers and school admins; set the download file name via the response. No repository evidence was supplied, so no specific paths or frameworks are assumed. Open non-blocking questions: Q1 (date format, timezone, separator) and Q4 (whether school admins are limited to the owning school; whether exports are audit-logged) must be raised with the product owner and the resulting choice documented; this ticket does not decide them.
criteria: An export request from an assigned teacher of the class and from a school admin succeeds and returns the CSV; requests from a student, a parent, and a teacher not assigned to the class are rejected with an authorization error and return no grade data.
The downloaded file name consists of the class's code and the current date, with a .csv extension.
Decisions or pending status for Q1 (date format/timezone/separator) and Q4 (admin school scope, audit logging) are recorded in the ticket before release.

work_items.title: Add role-gated 'Export CSV' button to the class gradebook page
work_items.description: Scope: UI change on the class gradebook page. Expected behavior: an 'Export CSV' button is shown that triggers download of the class's grades CSV via the W2 endpoint (R1). The button is rendered only for the class's assigned teachers and school admins; students and parents do not see it (R5). Bounded approach: use the same role information the page already has for the viewing user to decide rendering; server-side enforcement remains in W2, so hiding the button is not the only control. No repository evidence was supplied, so no component paths are assumed.
criteria: On the class gradebook page, an assigned teacher sees a button labeled 'Export CSV', and clicking it downloads a CSV file of that class's grades.
The 'Export CSV' button is rendered for assigned teachers and school admins and is not rendered for students or parents viewing any page where gradebook data is shown to them.

review_findings: CSV/formula-injection escaping is filed under Q5 as a non-blocking formatting detail. W1-AC5 lets it merge with a 'pending' status. Assignment titles and student names are user-controlled and are written into a file teachers open in spreadsheet tools, so this is a security concern for a tier-3 feature. It should be a requirement (safe_inference from S3) with a blocking security_check criterion, rather than a deferrable documentation item.

School-admin authorization scope is unresolved (Q4) but marked non-blocking. W2-AC1 accepts 'a school admin' without testing an admin from a different school. Q4 itself says restricting access to the owning school's admins is the safe interpretation, yet no requirement or criterion encodes it. That leaves a possible cross-school exposure of student grade data. Two remedies: add a criterion that rejects admins of other schools, or make Q4 blocking until a human answers it.

R2 requires 'exactly one row per enrolled student', while R8 excludes dropped students. Whether dropped students still count as 'enrolled' is left implicit. W1-AC1 quietly merges the two as 'enrolled, non-dropped'. R2 should state the exclusion or cross-reference R8, so a test of R2 alone cannot conflict with R8.

W3-AC2 extends the button-absence check to 'any page where gradebook data is shown to them' for students and parents. The source only concerns the class gradebook page. This criterion should be limited to the class gradebook page.

R7 says the file name is the class code plus today's date. However, W2-AC2's evidence only requires that the name 'contains' the class code and date, which is weaker than the criterion text 'consists of'. W2-AC2 also adds a .csv extension that the source never states. The evidence should assert the full expected name (or the pattern agreed under Q1), and the extension should be labelled as an inference.

R1 cites S7, which is only the teacher motivation statement. It is not a behavioral requirement. The 'downloads the class's grades as a CSV' behavior comes from S1 together with the file described in S2/S3. S7 adds no grounding for R1's behavior and could be dropped from R1's source_refs.

case.request: For our internal deploy CLI, please add a --dry-run flag to the `deploy` command. With --dry-run it should resolve the target environment, compute the same change plan it would normally apply (services to restart, config diffs, migrations to run), print that plan, and exit with code 0 without touching anything. If plan computation fails it should exit non-zero with the same error it would give in a real run. It should also work with the existing --output json option so CI can parse the plan. Add a line to the command's --help text. No changes to how a normal deploy behaves.
case.rationale: A bounded CLI flag with explicit behaviour, exit codes and output format.

requirements: The internal deploy CLI's `deploy` command accepts a new --dry-run flag.
With --dry-run, the command resolves the target environment and computes the same change plan a normal deploy would apply. The plan covers services to restart, config diffs and migrations to run.
With --dry-run, the command prints the computed change plan.
With --dry-run, when plan computation succeeds, the command exits with code 0.

A --dry-run invocation must not touch anything. It must not restart services, apply config changes or run migrations. The full set of other side effects that must be suppressed is pending clarification: deploy locks, audit or history writes, notifications, and state or cache writes during environment resolution.
With --dry-run, if plan computation fails, the command exits with a non-zero code and reports the same error it would give in a real run.
--dry-run works together with the existing --output json option, so that CI can parse the plan.
The `deploy` command's --help text includes a line describing --dry-run.
The behavior of a normal deploy (without --dry-run) is unchanged.

blocking_questions.question: What does 'without touching anything' cover beyond restarts, config application and migrations? Must a dry run avoid acquiring deploy locks, writing audit or deploy-history records, sending notifications, and writing state or cache during environment resolution? Should a dry run itself be recorded anywhere, for example in an audit log?
blocking_questions.why: This defines the safety semantics of a deploy tool. If environment resolution or planning currently acquires locks or mutates state, the dry-run path could have real side effects. It could also block, or be blocked by, concurrent real deploys. It also decides whether dry runs leave an audit trail. An authorized human must decide this; the implementer should not choose.

review_findings: S3 says the dry run must exit 0 'without touching anything'. R3 and AC1.4 narrow this to three executors: restart, config-apply and migration. They do not verify other side effects a deploy tool commonly has, such as deploy locks, audit or history writes, notifications, or state or cache writes during environment resolution. Q3 covers exactly this and is marked non-blocking. Its why_it_matters also pre-selects a default ('read-only, skip locks and history writes'), which effectively decides safety semantics without an authenticated answer. For a tier-3 deploy tool, this should be answered by a human, or R3/AC1.4 should explicitly assert no lock acquisition and no audit or history writes, before implementation.

No criterion covers R4 combined with R5: a plan-computation failure during `deploy --dry-run --output json`. It is unspecified whether the error must match the real run's JSON-mode error output and exit code. Also, AC3.1's 'stdout contains only valid JSON' is not checked on the failure path.

AC3.1 and the WI3 description require that stdout contain only valid JSON. S5 only says the option should 'work' so CI can parse the plan. The criterion is a reasonable inference, but it is not stated in the source. It may conflict with existing --output json conventions (for example, logs on stdout), which are unknown because no repository evidence was supplied.

Several criteria add specifics the source does not state. AC1.1 assumes a positional `<target>` argument syntax. AC1.2 requires the resolved environment name to appear in the output, but S2 only requires resolving the environment and printing the plan. AC2.1 requires an identical exit code and byte-identical text, while S4 says 'non-zero with the same error'. AC1.3 mandates a 'single shared plan-computation function', which is an implementation constraint derived from R8 (safe_inference). These should be reviewed as inferences, not presented as directly stated.

No repository or evidence IDs were supplied (A1), yet the criteria assume specific artifacts exist: an existing deploy test suite (AC1.5), mockable restart, config and migration executors (AC1.4), and an existing --output json mechanism reusable for the plan (WI3). If these do not exist, the criteria cannot be satisfied as written. Separately, R1 mentions 'internal deploy CLI', which comes from the part of S0 not captured in S1; the citation is incomplete but still traceable to S0.

WI1 says to 'branch after plan computation'. This assumes that plan computation and environment resolution have no side effects today. If the current code acquires locks or mutates state before or during planning, the dry-run path would touch things despite AC1.4 passing. The shared-logic refactor (R8/AC1.3) also risks changing normal deploy behavior (R7). AC1.5 mitigates this only if existing tests are comprehensive. Risk tier 3 must be kept.

Several open questions carry pre-decided defaults in why_it_matters and are delegated to the implementer or PR review rather than an authorized human: Q2 (JSON schema for CI consumers), Q4 (empty-plan behavior) and Q5 (help wording). Q4 and Q5 are low risk. Q2 affects a CI-facing contract and would benefit from an explicit answer. No answers have been fabricated, but defaults should not be treated as approved.

AC4.1 is labeled automated_test, but its evidence allows 'captured output', which is manual evidence; the verification kind is inconsistent. The candidate title is also a truncated copy of the objective rather than a concise title.

Prioritize the checkout improvement with the biggest expected impact among candidate options (e.g. redesign, faster payments, fewer steps).
Scope the plan so the team can begin work on Monday.
The checkout fix is expected to be delivered within the current sprint.

Handling and display of the additional employee data must comply with the obligations that apply to customers in both the US and the EU.

blocking_questions.question: Should skip-level managers see the additional fields for indirect reports, only for direct reports, or not at all? Should this be configurable per customer?

blocking_questions.why: This is a legal and compliance obligation for handling health-related personal data across jurisdictions.

case.request: Our streaming app needs an offline mode. Subscribers on flights and commutes keep asking for it and a competitor just launched downloads. We should support it on iOS and Android. We haven't worked out whether this is the whole catalogue or just our originals, since some licensed titles may not allow downloads, and product hasn't decided whether downloads are a premium-tier perk or available on every plan. Please break this down so engineering can start.

requirements: The streaming app shall provide an offline mode that lets subscribers download titles and play them back without a network connection, for example on flights and commutes.
Offline mode shall be supported in both the iOS and Android apps.
Download eligibility shall be limited to an approved catalogue scope. Whether that scope is the whole catalogue or only originals is undecided.
Titles whose licences do not permit downloads shall not be offered for download.
Access to downloads shall be gated by subscription plan according to a product decision. That decision could make downloads a premium-tier perk or make them available on every plan.

blocking_questions.question: Which titles can be downloaded: the whole catalogue, or only our originals? For licensed titles, who confirms which ones permit downloads, and how is that permission recorded?
blocking_questions.why: Offering downloads of titles whose licences forbid them creates legal and contractual exposure. The answer also changes the eligibility logic and the content metadata that must be built.

blocking_questions.question: Are downloads a premium-tier perk, or available on every subscription plan?
blocking_questions.why: This decides entitlement checks, billing and plan packaging. It also decides what happens to downloaded content when a subscriber changes plan, which affects revenue and what is built.

case.request: Bug in the clinic scheduling app: reminder emails show the wrong appointment time for appointments that fall after a daylight-saving change. Repro: in a clinic set to America/Chicago, on 1 March book an appointment for 10:00 on 12 March. The booking screen and calendar show 10:00 correctly, but the 24-hour reminder email says 11:00. Appointments booked after the DST switch are fine. Looks like the reminder job formats the time using the offset at booking time instead of the clinic's timezone at the appointment date. Expected: the email always shows the same local time as the calendar. Please fix and add a regression test covering both spring and autumn transitions.
case.rationale: Clear repro, expected behaviour and suspected cause make this directly actionable.

requirements: The 24-hour reminder email must always show the same local appointment time as the calendar, including for appointments that fall after a daylight-saving change from the booking date.
The reminder job must format the appointment time using the clinic's timezone rules as of the appointment date, not the UTC offset in effect at booking time.
Reminder times for appointments that do not cross a DST transition (e.g. booked after the DST switch) must remain correct after the fix.

Add a regression test covering both spring and autumn DST transitions, verifying the reminder email time matches the calendar local time (e.g. America/Chicago clinic, booked 1 March for 10:00 on 12 March shows 10:00).

work_items.title: Fix reminder job to format appointment time in clinic timezone at appointment date
work_items.description:
Scope: the clinic scheduling app's 24-hour reminder email path. Per the report (S4), the job appears to format the time with the UTC offset in effect at booking time. That makes appointments after a DST change show the wrong hour. Repro: an America/Chicago clinic books on 1 March for 10:00 on 12 March, and the email shows 11:00.

Expected behavior: the email shows the same local time as the calendar (S5). The time is derived from the appointment instant, converted using the clinic's IANA timezone rules as of the appointment date. Appointments that do not cross a transition keep showing the correct time.

Approach:
1. Locate the reminder job's time-formatting code.
2. Replace any stored or booking-time offset with a timezone-aware conversion using the clinic's configured timezone.
3. Reuse the same conversion the calendar uses if one exists.

No repository was supplied, so no file paths are asserted. Open, non-blocking questions for the implementer to report on rather than decide:
- Q1: whether SMS or other reminder intervals share this formatting path.
- Q2: whether already-queued reminders store a precomputed formatted time that would still be wrong after deploy.
- Q3: whether a timezone label should be shown. This is not in scope unless a human decides.
criteria: For a clinic in America/Chicago, an appointment booked on 1 March for 10:00 on 12 March produces a 24-hour reminder email showing 10:00, matching the calendar.

Reminder formatting no longer uses the offset captured at booking time. The displayed local time is computed from the appointment instant using the clinic's timezone rules effective on the appointment date.
Appointments booked and scheduled on the same side of a DST transition still show a reminder time equal to the calendar local time after the fix.

The implementer documents findings, without deciding scope, on:
- Q1: whether other channels or intervals share this formatting path.
- Q2: whether queued reminders store precomputed times.
The findings are attached for human review.

work_items.title: Add DST regression tests for reminder email time (spring and autumn)
work_items.description:
Scope: automated regression tests for the 24-hour reminder email time.

Coverage:
- Spring-forward case: the America/Chicago repro, booked 1 March for 10:00 on 12 March, must show 10:00.
- Autumn fall-back case: a booking made before the autumn transition for an appointment after it must show the calendar local time.
- Each test asserts that the reminder's displayed time equals the calendar's local time.

Approach:
- Use a fixed or injectable clock and a clinic timezone of America/Chicago.
- Place tests in the project's existing test suite for the reminder job.

No repository or test paths were supplied, so none are asserted. Depends on WI-1 so the tests pass against the fix.
criteria: A regression test covers a spring DST transition. For an America/Chicago clinic, booked 1 March for 10:00 on 12 March, it asserts the reminder email time is 10:00 and equals the calendar time.

A regression test covers an autumn DST transition. For an America/Chicago clinic, it books before the autumn fall-back for an appointment after it and asserts the reminder email time equals the calendar local time.
The regression tests are shown to detect the defect: they fail when run against the pre-fix formatting behavior.

review_findings: R2 and AC-1.2 turn the reporter's hedged root-cause guess (S4: 'Looks like the reminder job formats the time using the offset at booking time') into a binding implementation requirement. AC-1.2 requires a diff showing removal of a booking-time offset. If investigation finds a different cause, such as a stored pre-formatted string, a server-timezone default, or UTC arithmetic, this criterion cannot be satisfied as written, even when the user-visible outcome in R1/S5 is correct. Recommend making AC-1.2 conditional on the confirmed cause, or restating it as an outcome: timezone-aware conversion using the clinic timezone on the appointment date.

The spec does not cover DST edge-case local times. These are appointments in the skipped spring-forward hour (e.g. 02:30 on the transition day in America/Chicago) and in the repeated fall-back hour (01:00-01:59, which occurs twice). R1 says the email 'always' matches the calendar, but the regression tests (AC-2.1, AC-2.2) only cover appointments well clear of the transition. Consider an explicit criterion that ambiguous or nonexistent local times render identically to the calendar, or record this as an open question.

AC-1.1 (WI-1) and AC-2.1 (WI-2) verify the same scenario with the same evidence type: the America/Chicago clinic, booked 1 March for 10:00 on 12 March, shows 10:00, via automated test. This duplication may cause double-counting or confusion over which work item owns the spring repro test. Consider having AC-1.1 reference the WI-2 test, or differentiating the two.
AC-1.1 is labelled provenance 'directly_stated' but cites R2, which is a safe_inference requirement. The criterion's provenance should reflect its weakest cited requirement, or cite only R1.
AC-1.4 cites R1 and R2 but verifies neither. It is a documentation task about open questions Q1 and Q2. Citing functional requirements for an investigation note obscures traceability.

Q2 (already-queued reminders holding precomputed wrong times) directly affects whether R1 ('always shows the same local time') holds after deploy. It is marked non-blocking, and no acceptance criterion ensures pending reminders are correct. It remains patient-facing risk at tier 3. A human should decide whether this is in scope before approval. Risk tier 3 is appropriately retained.
S0/S1 refer to 'reminder emails' generally, but R1 narrows scope to the '24-hour reminder email'. The narrowing is acknowledged via Q1, but it is an interpretation rather than explicit source text.

case.request: Since the 3.8 billing release, customers who upgrade plans mid-cycle are charged proration based on actual calendar days in the month, whereas the old system used a flat 30-day month. About 1,200 accounts were affected over six weeks; the differences range from a few cents to roughly $40 either way. Finance thinks the new calculation is actually correct and the old one was wrong. Support wants us to restore the old behaviour and refund everyone. Please fix the bug and handle the affected accounts.
case.rationale: Stakeholders disagree on which behaviour is correct and how to remediate money already charged, so the fix itself is undefined.

requirements: Make mid-cycle plan-upgrade proration use a single approved calculation method (either actual calendar days in the month, as since the 3.8 release, or the previous flat 30-day month), replacing the current disputed behaviour as decided by an authorized human.

Remediate the accounts affected since the 3.8 billing release (about 1,200 accounts over six weeks, with differences from a few cents to roughly $40 in either direction) according to an approved remediation policy.

Identify every account that had a mid-cycle plan upgrade prorated since the 3.8 billing release and compute, per account, the difference between the calendar-day proration charged and the flat 30-day-month proration, including the direction of the difference.

blocking_questions.question: Which proration method is authoritative going forward for mid-cycle upgrades: the actual calendar-day calculation introduced in 3.8 (Finance's view) or the previous flat 30-day month (Support's request)? Is the calendar-day behaviour consistent with published customer terms?
blocking_questions.why: Finance and Support disagree; the answer determines whether any code change is made at all and whether the 3.8 behaviour is a bug. It also affects how customers are charged and may carry contractual obligations.

blocking_questions.question: How should affected accounts be remediated: refund everyone (as Support asks), refund or credit only overcharged customers, re-bill undercharged customers, or take no financial action? Should remediation be cash refunds or account credits, and is there any minimum-amount threshold?
blocking_questions.why: Differences go in both directions, from cents to about $40 across ~1,200 accounts; remediation moves money, is effectively irreversible, and requires Finance approval.

case.request: We need visibility into over-the-air firmware update reliability for our smart thermostats. Devices already emit ota_started, ota_completed and ota_failed telemetry events with device_model, from_version and to_version fields. Please build a dashboard in our existing Grafana showing daily update success rate (completed / started) broken down by device model and target firmware version, plus the top failure error codes. Add an alert to the firmware on-call channel if the failure rate for any model/version pair exceeds 5% over a rolling 24 hours with at least 200 attempts. Data retention can follow the existing telemetry policy.
case.rationale: Source events, metric definition, breakdowns and alert thresholds are all specified.

requirements: Build a dashboard in the existing Grafana showing daily update success rate (completed / started) broken down by device model and target firmware version.

Dashboard and alert metrics are derived from the existing ota_started, ota_completed and ota_failed telemetry events; device model is taken from device_model and target firmware version from to_version.
The dashboard shows the top failure error codes.
Add an alert to the firmware on-call channel that fires if the failure rate for any model/version pair exceeds 5% over a rolling 24 hours with at least 200 attempts.
Data retention for this work follows the existing telemetry policy.

blocking_questions.question: Which field or event carries the failure error code for ota_failed? The source lists only device_model, from_version and to_version. If no error-code field exists today, should one be added to device telemetry, or should the error-code panel be deferred?
blocking_questions.why: The top failure error codes panel cannot be built without an error-code field. Adding one would require device-side firmware or telemetry changes, which changes what is built.

blocking_questions.question: How is the alert failure rate defined: ota_failed / ota_started, or 1 - ota_completed / ota_started? Does an 'attempt' mean an ota_started event? How should in-flight updates or updates with no outcome within the 24-hour window be treated?
blocking_questions.why: The two formulas diverge whenever updates are in flight or never report an outcome. That changes when the alert fires and whether the 5% and 200-attempt thresholds can be verified.

review_findings: R1 is labeled explicit_source and cites only S1, but its clause 'Do not add new device-side instrumentation' is not in the source. S1 only says devices already emit the events. This is an inferred constraint mixed into an explicit_source requirement, which breaks the one-provenance-per-requirement rule. It also has a material effect downstream. WI3 and AC1.2 rely on it to forbid adding an error-code field, even though the requester asked for top failure error codes. Split the prohibition into its own safe_inference requirement or make it a human decision, rather than presenting it as stated.

Q2 (which field carries the error code, and how many top codes to show) is marked non-blocking, but R4 cannot be delivered without it. The events are listed only with device_model, from_version and to_version. AC3.2 can be satisfied by 'a report that no such field exists', so WI3 could close without delivering the requested panel. AC3.1 also does not define the top-N count. Q2 should block WI3, or the acceptance criteria should not treat a no-field report as fulfilling R4.

Q3 (failure-rate formula, what counts as an attempt, and how in-flight updates are treated) is marked non-blocking, yet the blocking criteria AC4.1 and AC4.2 test the 5% and 200-attempt thresholds that depend on it. The formulas ota_failed/ota_started and 1 - completed/started diverge whenever updates are in flight or have no outcome. Letting the implementer choose and 'flag for confirmation' amounts to deciding an unanswered product question. Q3 should be blocking for WI4, or the thresholds cannot be verified.

Q4 (the exact firmware on-call channel and contact point) is non-blocking, but AC4.1 requires the notification to reach that channel. Without the answer, the destination is either guessed or AC4.1 cannot pass. Q4 is effectively a prerequisite for completing WI4.

AC4.1 requires a notification delivery record in the firmware on-call channel. Testing against the live on-call destination could page responders with false alerts. The criterion should specify a test or silenced contact point, or require coordination with on-call.

The daily success rate (completed/started per day) in R3 and AC2.2 does not say how to handle updates that start on one day and complete on the next. Daily ratios can then exceed 100% or be skewed. Q5 covers only the timezone, not this attribution rule. The same in-flight issue as Q3 applies to the dashboard metric.

R7 (a safe_inference that the alert is evaluated per model/version pair) largely restates R5, which is explicit_source and already says 'any device model / target firmware version pair'. AC4.3 and AC4.4 partly duplicate AC4.1 and AC4.2. Consider merging R7 into R5 or narrowing it to what is genuinely inferred, such as separate alert instances per pair.

R3 and the work items interpret 'target firmware version' as to_version. This is a reasonable inference, but it is presented under explicit_source. Similarly, AC1.1 adds a from_version grouping capability that the source does not request for any output. These are minor, but they are interpretation rather than stated fact.
The candidate title is a truncated copy of the objective ending in '...' rather than a concise title. This is cosmetic, but it reduces clarity for handoff.

case.request: Marketing wants to start tracking what people do across our online store, both the website and the iOS/Android apps, so they can build audiences and retarget them on ad platforms like Meta and Google. They'd like it as detailed as possible: page views, searches, cart activity, maybe even what people type into the search box before submitting. We sell in the US, UK and Germany. There is no consent banner on the site today. Can you turn this into tickets?
case.rationale: Sharing behavioural data with ad platforms in the UK and EU without a consent mechanism is a legal decision that must be made before anything is built.

requirements: Track page view events on the online store website and the iOS and Android apps.
Track search events on the online store website and the iOS and Android apps.
Track cart activity events on the online store website and the iOS and Android apps.
Make tracked behaviour available for building audiences and retargeting them on ad platforms such as Meta and Google.
Optionally capture search-box input typed before the user submits the search (requested tentatively with 'maybe').
Tracking must operate for users in the US, UK and Germany, the markets the store sells in, and must account for the absence of any existing consent banner on the site.

blocking_questions.question: What consent and legal-basis approach is approved for tracking and ad-platform sharing in each market (e.g. a consent management banner/prompt for UK and German users before non-essential tracking, US opt-out of sale/sharing handling, iOS App Tracking Transparency), and who (legal/privacy) signs off?
blocking_questions.why: There is no consent banner today and the store serves UK and German users; retargeting tracking and sharing with Meta/Google involves personal data and legal obligations. This determines whether tracking can be enabled at all, what must be built first, and whether events may fire before consent.

blocking_questions.question: Is capturing what users type into the search box before submitting approved, and if so with what limits (e.g. excluding or redacting personal data, debounce, retention)?
blocking_questions.why: Pre-submit keystroke capture is highly invasive, may collect personal data users never intended to send, and raises significant privacy-law risk; it changes what is built.

blocking_questions.question: What data and identifiers may be shared with Meta and Google (e.g. pixels/SDKs vs server-side conversions APIs, hashed emails, device IDs, user IDs), and what are the data minimisation and retention rules given the request for 'as detailed as possible'?
blocking_questions.why: Determines how personal data leaves the company to third parties, the integration architecture, and compliance obligations; sharing is hard to reverse.

case.request: Our developer platform's login endpoint (POST /api/session) has no brute-force protection. Please add: after 5 failed password attempts for the same account within 15 minutes, lock that account's password login for 15 minutes and send the account owner an email saying so. Separately, limit any single IP to 20 login attempts per minute across all accounts. Both limits return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header and a generic message that does not reveal whether the account exists. Log every lockout to the existing security audit log. SSO logins are out of scope. Use the Redis instance we already run for rate limiting.
case.rationale: Thresholds, responses, notifications, logging and scope exclusions are explicit.

requirements: Apply brute-force protection to the password login endpoint POST /api/session.
When the same account has 5 failed password attempts within 15 minutes, lock that account's password login for 15 minutes.
When an account is locked, send the account owner an email telling them the account's password login has been locked.
Limit any single IP address to 20 login attempts per minute, counted across all accounts. This limit is separate from the per-account lockout.
When either the account lockout or the IP rate limit applies, return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header. Include a generic message that does not reveal whether the account exists.
Record every account lockout in the existing security audit log.
Exclude SSO logins from the lockout and rate-limiting behaviour.
Store rate-limiting and lockout counters and state in the existing Redis instance.
During an active lockout, reject password login attempts for that account even when the password is correct.
review_findings: Q4 (handling of non-existent accounts) is marked non-blocking, but it decides whether R5's explicit requirement (responses must not reveal account existence) can be met. If real accounts lock and return 429 while non-existent accounts never do, lockout behaviour itself enumerates accounts. AC4.2 only compares lockout 429 bodies with IP-limit 429 bodies. It does not compare responses for existing and non-existing accounts under repeated failures, so W4 could pass while still leaking existence. Either make Q4 blocking, or add a criterion requiring indistinguishable behaviour (status, body, Retry-After and timing) for existent and non-existent accounts.

Window semantics are inconsistent. W2's approach, a per-account counter with a 15-minute TTL-based window, describes a fixed window. R2/S2 ('5 failed attempts within 15 minutes') and AC2.2 ('no 5 fall within any 15-minute window') imply a sliding window. With a fixed counter, failures at t=0,14,16,17,18,19 min never lock the account even though 5 fall inside [14,29]. AC2.2 only tests the negative case, so this under-enforcement would pass. The same fixed-vs-sliding ambiguity applies to the per-IP 'per minute' limit in R4/AC3.1. Neither Q2 nor Q7 captures this.

Q5 (whether to fail open or fail closed when Redis is unavailable) is security-critical and must be decided for W1 to be implemented. It is marked non-blocking, and no acceptance criterion covers Redis-outage behaviour. W1 could be delivered with an arbitrary failure mode. Add a criterion once Q5 is answered, or treat Q5 as gating W1 completion.

The per-account lockout lets any attacker who knows an account identifier lock the owner out with 5 wrong passwords, repeatable every 15 minutes. Each lockout also emails the owner. This denial-of-service and harassment vector is not listed among the risk reasons. Q6 only partly covers it (email flooding).

Q3 (how the client IP is derived behind proxies) is marked non-blocking. If X-Forwarded-For is trusted naively, R4 can be trivially evaded. If the proxy IP is used, all users share one limit. No acceptance criterion constrains how the IP is derived.

Several acceptance criteria are labelled 'directly_stated' but add constraints not in the source. AC5.1 and AC6.1 ('exactly one' email or entry; no email without a lockout). AC1.1 ('before credential verification completes', which derives from the R9 inference). AC4.1 (Retry-After no greater than the remaining block time). AC1.2 asserts SSO never touches the IP counter, although S4 says 'login attempts across all accounts'. These should be labelled as inferences.

Several behaviours are unspecified and untested. First, the response to the 5th failing attempt itself: 401 or 429? AC2.1 only covers the 'next' attempt. Second, which Retry-After value applies when both the lockout and the IP limit are active. Third, whether failed attempts during an active lock extend it or trigger another email. The last point is only partly covered by Q7.

R1 narrows S1's 'login endpoint' to 'password login endpoint'. The narrowing is consistent with S2 and S7, but it is not stated in S1. The title is a truncated copy of the objective ending in '...'. The risk reasons retain the stale 'Unclassified input' entry. These are minor clarity issues; risk tier 3 must remain.

W2 and W3 must reject requests, but the shared 429 response builder is in W4, which depends on both. As a result, W2 and W3 are delivered with an undefined rejection format that W4 must later retrofit. Consider making W4 a foundation that W2 and W3 depend on, or state an interim rejection contract.

case.request: Our clinics want front desk staff and our external billing contractors to be able to open patient records from their personal laptops and phones so they can work from home a couple of days a week. Right now the scheduling and records system is only reachable from clinic workstations on the office network. Can we open it up so they can log in from anywhere? The contractors are a third-party firm we started using last month.
case.rationale: Opening patient data to a third party on unmanaged devices depends on access scope and contractual/regulatory decisions nobody has stated.

requirements: Front desk staff must be able to open patient records in the scheduling and records system from their personal laptops and phones.
External billing contractors, who belong to a third-party firm, must be able to open patient records in the scheduling and records system from their personal laptops and phones.

The scheduling and records system, currently reachable only from clinic workstations on the office network, must be reachable for login from outside the office network (e.g. from home) by the permitted users.
Remote access must require users to log in (authenticate) before they can open patient records.

blocking_questions.question: Is a Business Associate Agreement (or equivalent data processing/confidentiality agreement required under the applicable health privacy law) in place with the third-party billing contractor firm, and which regulatory regime (e.g. HIPAA) governs these patient records?
blocking_questions.why: Granting a third party access to patient records without the required legal agreement may be a compliance violation; this determines whether contractor access can be built at all.

blocking_questions.question: What data and functions may each role access remotely? For example, should billing contractors see only billing-relevant fields rather than full clinical records, and should front desk staff be limited to scheduling and demographic data?
blocking_questions.why: Determines the access control model and which personal health data is exposed to which users (minimum-necessary access).

blocking_questions.question: Are unmanaged personal laptops and phones acceptable, or must devices meet requirements (device management enrollment, disk encryption, OS patch level, screen lock), and must local download, printing, or caching of patient data be prevented?
blocking_questions.why: Personal devices outside clinic control create a risk of patient data leakage; the answer changes the architecture (e.g. managed devices vs. virtual desktop or browser-only access with no local storage).

blocking_questions.question: How should the system be reached remotely: exposed directly to the public internet, or only through a VPN, zero-trust access gateway, or remote desktop service? Does 'from anywhere' include locations outside the country, and are there IP or geographic restrictions?
blocking_questions.why: Exposing a patient records system to the internet is a significant, hard-to-reverse security decision that shapes the network design.

blocking_questions.question: What authentication is required for remote users (e.g. mandatory multi-factor authentication, single sign-on through the clinic identity provider), how are contractor accounts provisioned, and who is responsible for revoking access when a contractor leaves or the engagement ends?
blocking_questions.why: Determines who may access patient records and how third-party access is controlled over its lifecycle.

case.request: Reporting needs a reliable delivery timestamp. Add a nullable delivered_at_utc column to the shipments table in Postgres. For new shipments, set it when the shipment status changes to DELIVERED, using the timestamp of that status event converted to UTC. Backfill existing rows from the shipment_events table (latest DELIVERED event per shipment); shipments never delivered stay null. The backfill must run in batches of 10,000 rows, be safe to re-run, and not lock the table, since the table has about 80 million rows and is written to constantly. Add an index on the new column. Reports will switch to it in a later ticket.
case.rationale: Schema, population rule, backfill source and operational constraints are all specified.

requirements: Add a nullable column named delivered_at_utc to the shipments table in Postgres.

When a shipment's status changes to DELIVERED, set delivered_at_utc to the timestamp of that status event, converted to UTC. The rule for repeated DELIVERED events, and for shipments that leave DELIVERED, is pending Q1.
Backfill delivered_at_utc for existing shipments from the shipment_events table, using the latest DELIVERED event per shipment, converted to UTC.
Shipments that were never delivered keep delivered_at_utc as null.
The backfill runs in batches of 10,000 rows.
The backfill is safe to re-run. Repeated executions produce the same result without corrupting data.
The backfill must not lock the shipments table, because the table has about 80 million rows and is written to constantly.
Add an index on the delivered_at_utc column.

The column addition and index creation should avoid prolonged locks that block writes to the constantly written shipments table. Any unavoidable brief lock must be bounded, for example by lock_timeout, and the index should be built without blocking writes.

blocking_questions.question: How should delivered_at_utc behave when a shipment receives more than one DELIVERED event, or changes from DELIVERED to another status? Options include: keep the first DELIVERED timestamp, update to the latest, or clear the column. Should the live rule match the backfill rule (latest DELIVERED event)?
blocking_questions.why: This defines what the reporting column means. The backfill is fixed to the latest DELIVERED event. A different live rule would give reporting inconsistent semantics. It would also make the backfill's overwrite and re-run logic contradict values set live.

review_findings: Q3 (repeated DELIVERED events or leaving DELIVERED) is marked non-blocking and left to the implementer, but it decides what the column means. S3 fixes the backfill to the latest DELIVERED event. The live-update rule in R2/W2 is undefined. W3's approach allows overwriting rows 'where the value differs from the computed value'. W3-AC3 forbids overwriting values set live by W2. If W2 keeps the first DELIVERED timestamp, or clears the column when a shipment leaves DELIVERED, then W3-AC1 (0 mismatches against the latest DELIVERED event) and W3-AC3 contradict each other. Reporting would also get inconsistent semantics. This needs a human decision, or an explicit shared rule applied to both W2 and W3, before the criteria can be met.

Q2 says the source timestamp semantics 'can be determined from the existing schema'. If shipment_events uses timestamp without time zone, the implied zone cannot be read from the schema. It is a business fact that needs a human or evidence. A wrong assumption would corrupt the UTC conversion for about 80 million backfilled rows and all live rows. No repository evidence was supplied to support settling this without escalation.

S2/R2 say 'for new shipments', but W2 applies the rule to any shipment that receives a DELIVERED event. It is unclear whether 'new' means shipments created after deployment or deliveries occurring after deployment. Under the narrower reading, shipments already in flight that are delivered after the backfill finishes would never be populated. The candidate silently adopts the broader reading without recording it as an inference or a question.

Assumption A2 delegates all open questions (Q1-Q4) to the implementer. Several of them (Q2, Q3, Q4) affect data correctness for a production table of about 80 million rows. There are no authenticated answers. Delegating behavioral decisions to implementation is not a safe substitute for clarification on tier-3 data-mutation work.

R4 and S4 require batches of 10,000 rows. W3 proposes primary-key ranges of 10,000, which yield fewer rows wherever keys have gaps. W3-AC2 only checks 'at most 10,000', which loosens the stated requirement. It is also unclear whether a batch means 10,000 scanned rows or 10,000 updated rows. The criterion should state the interpretation explicitly.

No criterion addresses the coverage gap between W2 deployment and backfill completion. The backfill's NULL-only or differs logic and its sequencing are only suggested in the description. The ordering 'deploy W2 before running the backfill' is expressed only as the W3-depends-on-W2 dependency, with no verifiable criterion.

W4 allows the index to be built before the backfill. The backfill would then update about 80 million rows while maintaining the index, increasing write amplification and WAL volume. Neither choice is required by the source, but the risk is not captured in the risk reasons or in the criteria.

R8 extends the S4 non-locking constraint, which the source states only for the backfill, to the column migration and the index build. This is correctly labelled safe_inference. However, W1-AC2 and W4-AC2 are blocking criteria that rest only on inference, and ADD COLUMN still takes a brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so 'without blocking writes' must be read as 'bounded by lock_timeout'. W4-AC2 lacks a similarly bounded wording.

R9 is a scope exclusion (reports are deferred) but is classified as a 'functional' requirement. It is also attached to W1 with a documentation criterion. It is not a behavior to implement and could be recorded as an exclusion rather than a requirement.

W2-AC3 is classified as documentation but also requires a test for a second DELIVERED event. The expected outcome of that test is unspecified because Q3 is unresolved, so the criterion cannot be objectively verified.

The first risk reason, 'Unclassified input held at maximum risk until reviewed', is stale now that the input has been classified. Tier 3 remains appropriate given the production schema change and the mass data mutation. The reviewer does not lower risk.

case.request: Our recruiting product has kept every candidate profile, CV and interview note since launch, about 4 million candidates across customers in the US, UK and EU. Storage costs are climbing and a couple of enterprise customers have asked whether we comply with privacy rules on retention. Please set up an automated job to purge old candidate data. Some customers have mentioned that candidates involved in ongoing disputes need to be kept, but we don't have a flag for that yet.
case.rationale: Deleting candidate data is irreversible and the retention period, deletion method and hold exemptions are all unstated.

requirements: Provide an automated job that purges old candidate data.
The purge scope covers candidate profiles, CVs and interview notes.
Candidates involved in ongoing disputes must be kept and excluded from purging.
Introduce a mechanism (e.g. a flag) to mark candidates involved in ongoing disputes so the purge job can exclude them, since no such flag exists today.
Retention and purge behaviour must comply with applicable privacy retention rules for customers in the US, UK and EU.
The purge job must run automatically on a recurring basis without manual triggering and handle a data volume of roughly 4 million candidates.
Purging should reduce storage consumed by retained candidate data.

blocking_questions.question: What makes candidate data 'old'? What retention periods apply per data type (profile, CV, interview note), per jurisdiction (US, UK, EU), and are they set globally by us or configurable per customer (as data controller)?
blocking_questions.why: Determines exactly which personal data is irreversibly deleted and whether deletion meets legal retention obligations in each jurisdiction and customer contract.

blocking_questions.question: How are candidates in ongoing disputes identified, who is authorised to set and clear the dispute/hold flag, and must purging be withheld entirely until the flag exists and is populated?
blocking_questions.why: Purging disputed candidates before a hold mechanism exists could irreversibly destroy data customers are legally required to keep.

blocking_questions.question: What does 'purge' mean: hard deletion, anonymisation, or soft delete with a grace period? Must it also cover backups, search indexes, analytics copies, attachments storage and any third-party processors?
blocking_questions.why: Deletion is irreversible and the method determines privacy compliance and what systems must be changed.

blocking_questions.question: How should the existing backlog since launch be handled on first run: must customers be notified or opt in, and is legal/privacy sign-off required before enabling the job?
blocking_questions.why: The first run could delete a large share of ~4 million candidates' data irreversibly and affects contractual and compliance obligations to customers.

case.request: We want to launch digital gift cards on the web store before the holidays. Shoppers can buy a gift card for $25, $50 or $100, pay with any existing payment method, and have it emailed to a recipient with an optional message. Each card gets a unique 16-character code. Recipients redeem the code at checkout; partial redemption is allowed and the remaining balance stays on the code. Cards don't expire. Add a public balance-check page where you enter a code and see the remaining balance, rate-limited to prevent code guessing. Finance needs a daily report of cards sold, redeemed and outstanding liability.
case.rationale: A well-specified feature spanning purchase, delivery, redemption, balance lookup and reporting that naturally splits into several tickets.

requirements: Shoppers can purchase digital gift cards on the web store.
Gift cards are offered only in the fixed denominations of $25, $50 and $100.
Shoppers can pay for a gift card with any existing web store payment method.
A purchased gift card is delivered by email to a recipient that the shopper specifies.
The shopper may optionally include a message, which is sent with the gift card email.
Each gift card is assigned a unique 16-character code.
Recipients can redeem a gift card code at web store checkout.
Partial redemption is allowed, and any remaining balance stays on the code for future use.
Gift cards and their balances do not expire.
A public balance-check page lets anyone enter a code and see its remaining balance.
The balance-check page is rate-limited to prevent code guessing.
Finance receives a daily report of gift cards sold, gift cards redeemed and outstanding gift card liability.
When a code is invalid, the balance-check response discloses only that the code is invalid and nothing more.
Code entry at checkout is also protected against code guessing, so it cannot be used to bypass the balance-check rate limit.
A redemption can never deduct more than the card's remaining balance, and a balance can never go below zero.
Gift card codes are generated so they are not predictable or sequential.
A recipient email address is required when purchasing a gift card.
Every issuance and redemption is recorded with its amount and time, so balances and the daily report can be derived.
The gift card feature must be launched before the holidays.

blocking_questions.question: At checkout, how should gift cards combine with the order total and other payment? Specifically: can a gift card be combined with another payment method when its balance is below the order total? Can multiple gift cards be used on one order? When the balance exceeds the order total, is only the order total deducted?
blocking_questions.why: This decides the core redemption and money-handling behavior. Without it, the partial-redemption and over-balance outcomes are not deterministically buildable or testable.

blocking_questions.question: How are refunds, chargebacks and cancellations handled? This covers both gift card purchases (for example, after the code was delivered or partly used) and orders paid partly or fully with a gift card. How does each case affect card balances and reported liability?
blocking_questions.why: This decides how money and stored value are adjusted. It also determines whether liability can be calculated as issued minus redeemed.

blocking_questions.question: Which jurisdictions, currencies and gift card regulations apply? This includes non-expiry rules, unclaimed property or escheatment obligations, and required disclosures. Has legal or compliance review approved non-expiring cards?
blocking_questions.why: Non-expiring stored value creates long-term legal and financial obligations that are costly to reverse after launch.

blocking_questions.question: How long should recipient email addresses and gift messages be retained? Who may access them, and are they subject to deletion requests or content moderation?
blocking_questions.why: Recipient emails and messages are third-party personal data that is collected without the recipient's direct consent.

review_findings: W5-AC1 requires an end-to-end test that partially redeems a card before checking its balance. Partial redemption is delivered by W4, but W5 lists only W1 as a dependency. Either add a W5→W4 dependency or change the evidence to seed the balance directly in the ledger.

Q1 (split tender and multiple cards per order) is marked non-blocking, yet it governs the core checkout behavior. Partial redemption per S7 is only meaningful when either the card balance exceeds the order total or the remainder can be paid another way. W4-AC3 says an over-balance deduction is 'capped or rejected', which leaves the observable behavior undecided and not deterministically testable. Q1 should be blocking for W4, or the AC must pick one behavior with human sign-off.

W2-AC3 requires a successful purchase with 'each payment method currently supported by the web store'. Once W4 ships, that set would include gift cards, which directly contradicts leaving Q2 open. The AC should explicitly exclude or defer gift-card-as-tender until Q2 is answered.

No repository or evidence was supplied. W2-AC3 (one test per existing payment method), W2's 'existing payment integration' and W3's 'existing email capability' all assume systems whose existence and scope are unverified. The set of existing payment methods is unknown, so the evidence cannot yet be enumerated.

The checkout redemption endpoint (W4) accepts codes and distinguishes valid, unknown and zero-balance codes. This makes it an enumeration oracle that bypasses the balance-page rate limit. Redemption rate limiting is deferred under non-blocking Q4, and no requirement covers it. This undermines the anti-guessing intent of S10.

S11 says 'cards ... redeemed'. W6 interprets this as 'amount redeemed' and adds 'count and value' for cards sold. Whether Finance wants redemption counts, amounts or both is unconfirmed.

W6-AC1 also hard-codes liability as 'total issued minus total redeemed'. That formula is only valid if refunds, chargebacks and cancellations never adjust balances, and Q3 leaves those open. The reconciliation criterion may therefore be wrong once Q3 is answered.

S1's timeline constraint 'before the holidays' is not captured as a requirement or constraint; it appears only in W2's prose. The concrete target date is unspecified, and no unresolved question asks for it, despite its effect on scope and sequencing.

Several work item descriptions contain behavior that is not captured as requirements with provenance:
- W5: invalid-code responses reveal nothing beyond invalidity.
- W3: the recipient email is required and validated.
- W1: a card 'status' field with undefined states.
- W4: a redemption ledger entry.

These are reasonable inferences but should be explicit safe_inference requirements, or be removed from the descriptions.

W5-AC2 is defined in terms of the 'same client' and a 'window reset'. The client key (IP, session or device) and the window are open under Q4, so the criterion cannot be verified as a product behavior until Q4 is resolved.

Non-expiring stored value creates long-term legal and regulatory liability (unclaimed property/escheatment, gift card laws, currency and region scope). Q8 raises this but is marked non-blocking. Recipient email addresses and messages are personal data, and their retention (Q7) is also non-blocking. Legal/compliance review should gate launch.

Tier 3 risk must be retained. This review cannot lower it or approve the work.
The candidate title is a truncated sentence ending in '...'. It should be a concise, complete title.

case.request: Automate new-hire onboarding in our HR platform. When a hire record moves to status 'Signed', automatically: (1) create the standard onboarding checklist from the template for their department; (2) post a Slack message to the hiring manager with the start date and a checklist link; (3) open an IT provisioning request in our existing ServiceNow queue with the hire's name, role, start date and department; (4) if any checklist item assigned to the manager is still open 3 business days before the start date, send the manager a reminder. If the start date changes, update the ServiceNow request and reschedule the reminder. Hires cancelled before start should close the checklist and the IT request.
case.rationale: Trigger, each automated step and the change/cancellation behaviour are specified, giving several separable tickets.

requirements: The onboarding automation is triggered automatically, within the HR platform, when a hire record transitions to status 'Signed'.
On trigger, create the standard onboarding checklist for the hire from the template associated with the hire's department.
On trigger, post a Slack message to the hire's hiring manager containing the start date and a link to the onboarding checklist.
On trigger, open an IT provisioning request in the existing ServiceNow queue containing the hire's name, role, start date and department.
If any checklist item assigned to the hiring manager is still open 3 business days before the hire's start date, send the manager a reminder.
When a hire's start date changes, update the corresponding ServiceNow IT provisioning request with the new start date.
When a hire's start date changes, reschedule the manager reminder relative to the new start date.
When a hire is cancelled before their start date, close the hire's onboarding checklist and the associated ServiceNow IT provisioning request.
The automation must link each hire record to its created checklist, ServiceNow request and scheduled reminder so later start-date changes and cancellations act on the correct artifacts.
No pending manager reminder is sent for a hire that has been cancelled before start.

work_items.title: Detect hire lifecycle events and persist hire-to-artifact links
work_items.description: Scope: the event-detection and linkage foundation for the onboarding automation in the HR platform. Behavior: detect when a hire record transitions to status 'Signed' (R1) and start the onboarding flow automatically. Also emit start-date-change and cancellation events for downstream tickets. Persist a link from each hire record to its created checklist, ServiceNow request and scheduled reminder (R9), so later changes act on the correct artifacts. Approach: implement one trigger adapter behind an interface plus a hire-artifact link store. Downstream tickets W2-W7 consume the events and write their artifact IDs into the store. Open items, not decided here: Q2 covers which HR platform is used and the detection mechanism (webhook, native workflow or polling). Q7 covers how a repeat transition back to 'Signed' is handled. The mechanism must not be assumed until Q2 is answered. No repository evidence was supplied.
criteria: A hire record transitioning to status 'Signed' starts the onboarding flow exactly once for that transition without manual action; a transition to any other status does not start it.
After the flow runs, the link store returns the checklist ID, ServiceNow request ID and reminder ID for the hire record, and start-date-change and cancellation events resolve to that same record.

work_items.title: Create department onboarding checklist from template on 'Signed'
work_items.description: Scope: checklist creation step. Behavior: when the W1 'Signed' event fires, create the standard onboarding checklist for the hire from the template associated with the hire's department (R2). Record the checklist ID and URL in the W1 link store. Approach: look up the template by the hire's department, then instantiate the checklist with its item assignees, including items assigned to the hiring manager. Open item, not decided here: Q6 covers behavior when a department has no template; this case must surface as an error and must not silently pick a default. Q7 (duplicate triggers) is also open.
criteria: For a hire in department D, the created checklist contains exactly the items of D's standard template with template-defined assignees, and its ID and link are stored against the hire.

work_items.title: Post Slack message to hiring manager with start date and checklist link
work_items.description: Scope: initial Slack notification. Behavior: on the 'Signed' trigger, post a Slack message to the hire's hiring manager (R3). The message contains the hire's start date and the link to the checklist created in W2. Approach: resolve the manager to a Slack user, then send the message through a Slack client wrapper that can be mocked in tests. Open item, not decided here: Q6 covers what happens if the manager cannot be mapped to a Slack user; this failure must be logged and visible.
criteria: On a 'Signed' trigger, exactly one Slack message is sent to the hiring manager's Slack user, and it contains the hire's start date and the URL of the checklist created for that hire.

work_items.title: Open ServiceNow IT provisioning request on 'Signed'
work_items.description: Scope: ServiceNow request creation. Behavior: on the 'Signed' trigger, open an IT provisioning request in the existing ServiceNow queue (R4). The request carries the hire's name, role, start date and department. Store the request ID in the W1 link store. Approach: build a ServiceNow client wrapper, then map the four fields into the request. Open item, not decided here: Q3 covers the queue or assignment group and the exact field mapping; these must be configuration values, not hard-coded guesses. This ticket transmits hire personal data to an external system.
criteria: On a 'Signed' trigger, one ServiceNow request is created in the configured existing queue with name, role, start date and department equal to the hire record's values, and its ID is stored against the hire.

work_items.title: Schedule manager reminder for open checklist items 3 business days before start
work_items.description: Scope: reminder scheduling and send. Behavior: schedule a check at 3 business days before the hire's start date (R5). When the check runs, if any checklist item assigned to the hiring manager is still open, send the manager a reminder. If none are open, send nothing. Store the reminder ID in the W1 link store. Approach: use a scheduled job keyed by hire, evaluate open manager-assigned items at execution time, and make the business-day calculation a replaceable component. Open items, not decided here: Q4 covers the business-day definition, holiday calendar, time zone and send time. Q5 covers the reminder channel. Q6 covers start dates already inside the 3-business-day window.
criteria: A reminder is scheduled at 3 business days before the start date. At execution it is sent to the manager only if at least one manager-assigned checklist item is open. No reminder is sent when all manager-assigned items are complete.

work_items.title: Handle start-date changes: update ServiceNow request and reschedule reminder
work_items.description: Scope: start-date change handling. Behavior: when W1 emits a start-date-change event, use the link store to find the linked artifacts. Update the linked ServiceNow request with the new start date (R6). Cancel the existing reminder and reschedule it relative to the new start date (R7). Approach: build a handler that consumes the change event and reuses the W4 client and W5 scheduler. Open items, not decided here: Q2 covers change detection. Q3 covers the field mapping. Q4 covers the business-day definition. Q6 covers a new date that falls inside the reminder window after a reminder was already sent.
criteria: After a start-date change, the hire's linked ServiceNow request shows the new start date, and no new ServiceNow request is created.
After a start-date change, the previous reminder is no longer scheduled, and exactly one reminder is scheduled at 3 business days before the new start date.

work_items.title: Handle pre-start cancellation: close checklist and IT request, suppress reminder
work_items.description: Scope: cancellation handling. Behavior: when a hire is cancelled before the start date, close the linked onboarding checklist and the linked ServiceNow IT provisioning request (R8). Ensure no pending manager reminder is sent for that hire (R10). Approach: build a handler that consumes the W1 cancellation event, closes both artifacts via the link store, and cancels the scheduled reminder. The reminder job also re-checks cancellation status at execution time. Open items, not decided here: Q2 covers cancellation detection. Q3 covers which ServiceNow state represents 'closed'; this must be a configuration value.
criteria: Cancelling a hire before the start date sets the linked checklist to closed and moves the linked ServiceNow request to the configured closed state. Cancellation on or after the start date does not trigger this handling.
After a pre-start cancellation, no manager reminder is sent for that hire, even if the reminder date passes with manager items still open.

review_findings: AC-W7-1 says cancellation on or after the start date does not trigger close handling, and labels this directly_stated. S8 covers only cancellation before start and says nothing about later cancellations. This negative behavior is an inference or product decision. Relabel it as safe_inference or raise it as an open question.

AC-W2-1 requires the checklist to use 'template-defined assignees', and W2 describes instantiating item assignees from the template. The source does not say where assignees come from. S6 only implies that some items are assigned to the manager. The assignment source is unstated, and R5's manager-item detection depends on it.

AC-W5-1 evidence asserts a schedule date for a start date following a weekend. This implicitly treats weekends as non-business days, which Q4 leaves undecided. The test should be parameterized on the business-day component, not bake in a definition.

Two criteria assume answers to open questions. AC-W1-1 requires the flow to start 'exactly once', which presumes an answer to Q7 on repeat transitions. AC-W6-2 requires exactly one rescheduled reminder, but Q6 has not decided what happens when the new date falls inside the window or after a reminder was sent. These criteria may conflict with eventual answers.

Q2, Q3 and Q5 are marked non-blocking, but W1 states the detection mechanism must not be assumed until Q2 is answered. W4 and W7 also need Q3's queue and closed state, and W5 cannot send a reminder without Q5's channel. The work items cannot be completed until these are answered.
